heading: Choosing a Broker: What Actually Matters
body: Brokerage/delivery charges, app reliability during volatile days, and how easy fund withdrawal is matter more day-to-day than flashy charting tools most beginners never use. Compare these three before anything else when picking where to open your demat account.

heading: Direct Mutual Fund Platforms
body: Apps that let you invest directly in Direct plans (skipping distributor commission) typically save you 0.5-1% a year in expense ratio versus going through a traditional advisor's Regular plan. That difference compounds meaningfully over a 15-20 year SIP.

heading: What to Check Before Opening a Demat Account
body: Look at the Annual Maintenance Charge (AMC), whether there's a minimum balance requirement, and how fast fund transfers settle after a sale. Account opening is usually free and instant via Aadhaar-based e-KYC these days — the ongoing charges are where platforms actually differ.

heading: Portfolio Tracker Apps: Worth Using?
body: A single dashboard that aggregates your mutual funds, stocks, EPF, and bank balances makes it far easier to do the quarterly net-worth check that actually matters, instead of logging into five different apps. Convenience here can be the difference between tracking consistently or not at all.

heading: SIP Auto-Debit vs Manual Investing
body: Platforms that support auto-debit SIPs remove the monthly decision entirely — the money leaves before you can second-guess it. If you've struggled with consistency, this one feature matters more than any other the platform offers.

heading: Checking a Broker's Downtime History
body: Every broker has had at least one high-volatility day where the app lagged or crashed. Before committing, search '<broker name> down' and '<broker name> complaint' to see how often and how recently it's happened — a pattern matters more than a single incident.

heading: Free vs Paid Research Tools
body: Most free screener tools (filtering stocks/funds by basic ratios) cover what a long-term investor actually needs. Paid research tools tend to add value for active traders making frequent short-term calls — think carefully about which category you actually are before paying for one.

heading: One-App Investing: Pros and Cons
body: Keeping stocks, mutual funds, and even insurance in one app is convenient, but it can make it harder to compare that app's recommended products against the wider market objectively. Occasionally cross-check a 'recommended' fund against a neutral source before acting on an in-app suggestion.

heading: Checking Exit Load and Lock-ins
body: Some funds charge an exit load (often 1%) if redeemed within a set period (commonly 1 year) — this fee isn't always obvious in the app's main screen. Always check the scheme details page for exit load and lock-in terms before investing, not after.

heading: Linking Your Bank for Faster Redemptions
body: Mutual fund redemptions typically settle in 1-3 working days once your bank account is properly linked and verified — unverified or newly added accounts can add extra delays right when you need the money. Double-check this link well before you actually need to withdraw.

heading: Comparing Account Opening Charges
body: Account opening is largely free across major Indian platforms now, so the real comparison point has shifted to annual maintenance charges, brokerage on trades, and how good customer support is when something goes wrong with a transaction.

heading: Two-Factor Authentication: Non-Negotiable
body: Always enable 2FA on any investing app, and never share OTPs with anyone claiming to be 'support' — legitimate support never needs your OTP. Most account-takeover fraud in investing apps traces back to a shared OTP, not a technical hack.
